name: scenescout
description: Exploratory UI testing: Claude explores a running web app like a curious user, finds what is broken or confusing, and writes a coverage-checked report.
long_description:
SceneScout gives Claude a real browser to test a web app with. Ask it to test an address, for example http://localhost:3000, and it visits the pages, tries the forms and buttons, notes what is broken or confusing, and writes a report. If you would rather not write a prompt, pick "Check my site" from the extension's prompts: a short form asks for the address, what to check and how careful to be, and Look only is the default. "File problems as tickets" files the problems you choose in GitHub or Jira after a preview, and only once you say yes in SceneScout's own form; the tracker's sign-in goes in this extension's settings, never in the chat.

Every request the page sends is checked against a write policy at the network layer. By default it refuses PUT, PATCH, DELETE and requests that look destructive, while ordinary form submissions (a plain POST) go through, so a form can still create a record or change one that was there, such as a saved profile. For a site that holds real data, ask it to observe only: then only GET, HEAD and OPTIONS requests leave the page, plus signing in, signing out and refreshing a token, and any POST you name as a read that does not look destructive. By default a link is opened like any page, so a link that changes something just by being opened, such as an unsubscribe link, is followed. Only HTTP is inspected: messages over a WebSocket are not. Only test apps you own or are authorised to test.

The test browser downloads on first use: the first test fetches it once (about 200 MB) and carries on. If that download fails, SceneScout says why and gives the command to run by hand: `npx -y scenescout install --browser-only`.

What it reaches: the site you test and whatever its pages load, Playwright's download servers once for the browser, and a model provider only if whoever runs it sets one up for the duplicate judge. It sends no telemetry. It keeps its notes, reports and saved sign-ins in a .scenescout folder in the project (Documents/SceneScout/<site> when there is no project), serves its live view on this computer only (127.0.0.1), and opens that and the report in your default browser. The full list: https://github.com/brunoboto96/SceneScout/blob/main/docs/guide/Ways-to-use-it.md#what-it-reaches

github_token.title: GitHub token (for filing tickets)
github_token.description: Only needed to file problems as GitHub issues. A token that can create issues in the repository. Kept by Claude Desktop and passed to SceneScout as GH_TOKEN; never shown in the chat.

jira_base_url.title: Jira site address (for filing tickets)
jira_base_url.description: Only needed to file problems in Jira, e.g. https://your-site.atlassian.net. Passed to SceneScout as JIRA_BASE_URL.

jira_email.title: Jira account email (for filing tickets)
jira_email.description: Only needed to file problems in Jira: the email of the account the API token belongs to. Passed to SceneScout as JIRA_EMAIL.

jira_api_token.title: Jira API token (for filing tickets)
jira_api_token.description: Only needed to file problems in Jira. Kept by Claude Desktop and passed to SceneScout as JIRA_API_TOKEN; never shown in the chat.

prompts.name: check-my-site
prompts.description: Start a guided check: a short form asks the address, what to check, how careful to be (Look only is the default) and how thorough; then the check runs and ends with each problem as a card. Never asks for a password.
prompts.text:
The person picked "Check my site". Run a guided SceneScout check for them, in plain words: they may not be technical, so never name a tool, a write mode or a setting to them.

1. Call scout_intake with no arguments. Where this app can show a form, the person chooses there: the address, what to check, how they sign in, how careful to be and how thorough. Follow what it returns: tell the person what the plan says to tell them, then make its calls in order. If it returns questions instead, ask them in one message and do as it says with the answers.
2. Never choose a care level for the person. "Look only" is the default. A care level that sends things to the site starts only once the person has confirmed it in the form the server shows them (scout_guided_confirm). You can ask for that form; you cannot answer it. If they go back, or the form cannot be shown, offer the same check in "Look only".
3. While it runs, call scout_status. Where this app draws the status pane, it shows the progress; otherwise post one short line in plain words every few steps saying what is happening.
4. When the check is done, call scout_cards and show each problem worst first: its picture, then its plain text.
5. Then offer what comes next, in these words: "Re-check after a fix", "Make a team report", "File problems as tickets", "Is it safe to run on my live site?".

Never ask for a password, a sign-in code or a token, and never type one yourself: when the site needs signing in, a browser window opens for the person to sign in as they normally would.

prompts.name: recheck
prompts.description: Check the problems earlier checks left open again, in the care level each was found in and never a looser one, and say which are gone, which are still there and which changed.
prompts.text:
The person picked "Re-check after a fix": "Check the open SceneScout problems again: call scout_recheck_plan, follow the plan it returns, and tell me which are gone."

1. Call scout_recheck_plan with no arguments. If it says no project is open, call it again with address: the site's address from this conversation, or ask the person for it. If the site needs signing in, pass signIn as the person's check used it. If it says there is nothing to check again, say so in a sentence and stop.
2. Follow the plan it returns as you would a guided check's: tell the person what it says to tell them, then make its calls in order. It runs in the care level the problems were found in, never a looser one. If it needs the person's confirmation, call scout_guided_confirm with its planId: you can ask for that form, you cannot answer it, and a confirmation an earlier check had does not carry over. If they go back, or the form cannot be shown, nothing is checked again: tell them so, in a sentence.
3. scout_verify lists each problem with its steps. Follow them, then record what you saw with scout_verify {id, verdict, note}: "gone", "present" (still there) or "changed". A problem whose steps need more than the plan's care level allows cannot be checked in it: leave it open, and tell the person it needs a check that may do more.
4. Call scout_cards with the ids you checked, and tell the person in plain words which are gone, which are still there and which changed. If the plan left problems for a re-check of their own, say so and offer it.

Never ask for a password, a sign-in code or a token, and never type one yourself: when the site needs signing in, a browser window opens for the person to sign in as they normally would.

prompts.name: team-report
prompts.description: Write the report in plain words, a page that opens in any browser, and say where it is. Nothing is sent anywhere.
prompts.text:
The person picked "Make a team report".

Call scout_team_report with no arguments. If it says no project is open, or "Not attached.", open one with scout_attach in mode "observe": the site's address and the folder SceneScout keeps its notes in, from this conversation, or ask the person for them. Then call it again. A report lists the problems of the check that ran in this conversation: if none ran, say so and offer "Check my site" first.
Tell them where it is: the page the result names (team-report.html, which opens in any browser), with the evidence folder beside it holding the pictures, the report as Markdown and a manifest of every file's SHA-256. Say it has a cover, each problem as a card, what was not checked and lines to sign off, and that it stays on this computer: nothing is sent anywhere.

prompts.name: file-tickets
prompts.description: Show the problems, preview the chosen ones as GitHub or Jira tickets, and file them only once you say yes in a form SceneScout shows you. The tracker's sign-in comes from the extension's settings, never from the chat.
prompts.text:
The person picked "File problems as tickets".

1. Call scout_cards and show the problems worst first, so the person can say which should become tickets. Note the ids of the ones they choose. If it says no project is open, or "Not attached.", open one with scout_attach in mode "observe": the site's address and the folder SceneScout keeps its notes in, from this conversation, or ask the person for them. Then call it again.
2. Ask where the team keeps its tickets, GitHub or Jira, and where in it, unless this conversation already says. For GitHub pass to "github", with target the repository as owner/name (such as acme/shop); for Jira pass to "jira", with target the project key (such as QA); the Jira site's address comes from SceneScout's settings.
3. Call scout_ticket_preview with the chosen ids, to and target. It sends nothing. Show the person what it lists: each ticket that would be filed, the ones already filed (which are not filed again), and any that wait for the next filing.
4. When they want them filed, call scout_ticket_file with the previewId it returned. SceneScout then shows the person a form listing the tickets, and files only if they say yes there. You can ask for that form; you cannot answer it. If they go back, turn it down or close it, tell them nothing was filed, and do not call it again unless they ask (it needs a new preview).
5. When it has filed them, show each ticket's link.

If the preview says there is no sign-in for the tracker, tell them, in these words: "SceneScout has no sign-in for GitHub or Jira yet. Whoever set it up adds one in the desktop extension's settings, or in the environment SceneScout starts in. Never paste it into the chat."
If this app cannot show the form, tell them, in these words: "This app cannot show the confirmation form, so tickets cannot be filed from here. A developer can file them from a terminal, after first seeing a list of what would be filed." Then give them the command for a developer to run in the project's folder, from a terminal:
   npx -y scenescout export --to github --repo owner/app
   (its sign-in comes from GH_TOKEN (or GITHUB_TOKEN) in that terminal's environment)
   npx -y scenescout export --to jira --jira-url https://your-site.atlassian.net --jira-project KEY
   (its sign-in comes from JIRA_EMAIL and JIRA_API_TOKEN in that terminal's environment)
   Without --yes it is a dry run: it lists what it would file and what is already filed, and creates nothing in the tracker. Adding --yes files them, each problem once. --only followed by the chosen ids, comma-separated, files just those; --project followed by the folder SceneScout keeps its notes in reads that folder.

Never ask for a token, and never pass one to a tool: if the person pastes one into the chat, tell them it should go in the extension's settings instead, and that they should replace it, since it has been shown.

prompts.name: is-it-safe
prompts.description: What each care level may and may not do on your site, word for word as the guided panel says it. Calls nothing.
prompts.text:
The person asked "Is it safe to run on my live site?". Reply with the text below, word for word, as separate paragraphs: add nothing, soften nothing and change nothing. Call no tool. Then offer "Check my site".

Look only, the default, opens pages and signs in. A search still runs, because all it does is open a page of results, but nothing that would save something is sent. Links are opened like any page, so a link that changes something just by being opened, such as an unsubscribe link, is not stopped. It is the safest choice for a live site.

May submit forms sends forms, and presses buttons that send something. What it sends can create a record, or change one that was there, as it would for anyone who sent it; deletes are blocked. On a site that is not on this computer, it asks you first.

May create test data creates the records it needs. What it sends can also change records that were there, but it deletes only what it created. It always asks you first, and is for a test copy only.

Deleting data that was already there is never offered here.

These limits are checked on every request your browser sends, not left to the AI's judgement. A request a care level does not allow never reaches your site. What a care level does allow, a form or a button, does on your site whatever it does for anyone who uses it.

It never asks for your password. When your site needs one, a browser window opens for you to sign in as you normally would.
